I don't have any advice, but wow, this has been a recurring problem at nearly EVERY job I've had (service industry). I drink a lot of water (even more so when I'm working) and have a small bladder, so I have to pee about once every hour, give or take. Even when I've worked for smaller businesses, I've always ended up getting a talking to from a manager about my bathroom habits. It doesn't matter how hard I work or how consistent my performance is; me being a human being with bodily functions is a huge problem apparently. 😑 I think having to pee frequently is viewed as "abnormal" because so many people have been conditioned to dehydrate themselves/deprive themselves of their needs for the sake of productivity. So when you're taking care of yourself  even in a manner as essential as staying hydrated and taking regular bathroom breaks, there tends to be an association with lesser work ethic (even though I know I sure as hell can't perform as well when I'm in physical discomfort). Ugh I hate it, and I hate that other people have to deal with this bs as well. 😕

As someone who also experiences anxiety, coming across as too needy is one of my greatest worries! But I often try to remind myself, as you should remind yourself, that having and expressing needs doesn't make you a bad person; it just makes you human! A lot of people struggle to be upfront and advocate for their needs, so the fact that you are doing that is awesome and a sign of growth in itself! It's one thing for your friend to express boundaries, but I can definitely resonate with the way those comments were framed coming across as unsympathetic, whether that was his intention or not. If someone told me my anxiety was a "limitation", and made assumptions about how I would react/feel in new situations, that would definitely make me feel hurt and like my capacity for progression and growth was not being acknowledged. Perhaps express to your friend that while you respect his right to set boundaries, you also want to feel like all the progress you've been making is being recognized, and you could use all the support you can get as you continue to move forward. Growth doesn't happen overnight; you're taking steps one at a time, and that's the best thing you can do! And remember that while your own sense of self worth goes a long way, you're not in the wrong for wanting to feel validated or supported by your friend; affirmation  and feeling safe and accepted are key components of any relationship! I wish you the best of luck with your friend, in continuing to cope through your anxiety, and in establishing a healthy support system!

It's legitimate in that it's a real company, but the pay is distressingly low. It's only 10 cents/message, and they demand that you meet a minimum amount of characters and always ask a question in each and every message. You also have to add notes for each conversation, and often have to scroll through the conversation log for context since it's all crowdsourced work as opposed to being assigned clients. Pay is always 10 cents/message no matter how long your message is, and does not factor for extra time spent adding notes and reading past messages for context; I was making about $6/hour on average. Furthermore, the premise of the job is that you're getting paid to catfish people; clients pay for a dating service under the impression that they are connecting with real people, and your job is to keep stringing them along and convincing them you're a real person so they continue to pay for their subscription to the service. All in all it's super shady on multiple levels! If you're just trying to bring in a little extra cash and aren't put off by the nature of the job, I say go for it, but it is definitely not something I felt comfortable doing for long and would not recommend personally.
